title: Competition Among China’s AI Models Is Intensifying as the Chip Sector Advances - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. The competition between makers of China’s artificial intelligence (AI) models is intensifying, raising questions among investors on the sustainability of leadership in model performance, with increasing focus on cost efficiencies and the harness layer.  At the same time, the country’s capacity for building semiconductors is showing signs of exceeding investor expectations, according to Goldman Sachs Research. Those insights were among the discussions at the second annual Goldman Sachs Asia Leaders Conference in Hong Kong, the firm’s largest client gathering in the region. The event featured companies that form the entire AI supply chain: 400 companies were represented and over 1,400 investors attended the event in Hong Kong. In many cases, the gap in performance, especially in coding, is narrowing between the leading AI models, says Ronald Keung, head of the Asia Internet Research team. “Intense competition on the model layer brings investor questions as to how AI-model developers can differentiate besides model performance,” Keung says. “The key may be in cost efficiencies and on the harness layer.” The harness layer refers to the ecosystem that houses and enables AI models. The harness allows the model to, among other things, access data and follow workflows. “The next key investments are focused more on the harness layer,” Keung says. “The AI labs in China actually are just beginning harness investments. In the past, the Chinese AI labs were more focused on the model layer.” Conference participants were also focused on China’s semiconductor sector, says Allen Chang, head of the Greater China Technology Research team. Officials in Beijing aim to increase the country’s self-sufficiency in AI and semiconductors. “There's always a lot of debate on China semiconductors,” Chang says. He says the development of China’s semiconductor industry—which includes chip design, tools for semiconductor manufacturing, silicon wafer fabrication, and the manufacturing of specialized AI chips—is progressing faster than he and the market expected. “The progress has surprised the market,” Chang says of China’s semiconductor industry. He points out that the local leading chip foundries in China have larger capacity expansion plans than analysts expected. At the same time, the semicap equipment makers (the tools for making semiconductor chips) have issued guidance for 40% year-on-year revenue increases over the next few years. Investors have noted that more of the makers of specialized computing chips for AI, the GPUs and ASICs, are listing shares on the public market, Chang says. “That’s why they need to announce their volumes in terms of production as well as technology migration,” he says. But even as the semiconductor industry advances, Chang says there are still bottlenecks—principally in the availability of GPUs. “Everything is driven by the GPU computing power.” And while there’s been progress, there are still constraints in terms of local foundry capacity and semicap equipment, he adds. Optical networking was another part of the AI ecosystem that was in focus at the conference, Chang says. Networking unlocks computing capability for AI chips and enables data exchange at low latencies. While copper cables and printed circuit boards are commonly used for short distance connections within servers, optical fiber connections have higher performance for long-distance or high-speed interconnections, according to Goldman Sachs Research. Our analysts expect the total addressable market for this technology to increase by nine times to $154 billion in 2028. As the technology advances, investors may not fully appreciate the success that Chinese models have had in proliferating around the world, Keung says. While China’s AI technology faces geopolitical scrutiny in some jurisdictions, adoption is ongoing. He notes that Chinese open-weight large language models (LLMs) are being housed on US hyperscaler cloud systems, which could mark a step forward for these models reaching larger markets. By keeping their data and computing on domestic servers, countries with higher security thresholds could allow the use of Chinese AI models. “We're seeing that as an interesting development,” Keung says. In the meantime, China’s AI companies are taking different approaches to creating a competitive advantage, Keung says. Some are pushing for premium frontier status—to create the most advanced models—while others are attempting to be more cost efficient. “What the labs are trying to aim for is the best price-to-performance ratio,” he says. “Our view is the combination of these elements will lead to pricing power,” Keung says. “Cost efficiencies and the strongest financial power will lead to the most lasting success.” This document has been prepared by the Goldman Sachs Executive Office and is not a product of Goldman Sachs Global  Investment Research. title: Forget The Chevelle, This 2028 Buick Riviera Restomod Looks Absolutely Ruthless - HotCars
content: Subscribe to the HotCars newsletter to never miss an update A grille wide enough to intimidate a modern pickup truck, headlights that look ready to interrogate oncoming traffic, and a stance that would make speed bumps a proper concern.     Buick certainly knew how to make an entrance in the '60s, but this interpretation takes that attitude a touch further. This 1965 Buick Riviera GS restomod rendering reimagines one of Detroit's greatest luxury     Muscle Cars with modern performance styling, a brilliant stance, and enough visual appeal to embarrass some of the newer lot. When Buick introduced the Riviera in 1963, its objective was to challenge the     Ford Thunderbird's dominance of America's personal luxury car segment. Under the direction of legendary     General Motors designer Bill Mitchell, the Riviera adopted a dramatically different approach to American luxury. Its long hood, sweeping rear fenders, and clean bodywork gave it an almost European grand touring appearance. The design reached its peak in 1965, when Buick introduced vertically concealed headlights behind distinctive clamshell covers, creating one of the most recognizable front ends in Detroit's history. The real excitement arrived with the introduction of the 1965     Buick Riviera Gran Sport, or GS. Underneath its elegant bodywork sat a massive 425 Super Wildcat Nailhead V8 making 360 horsepower and 465 lb-ft of torque. Equipped with dual four-barrel carburetors, the engine was reportedly effortless and accompanied by the unmistakable soundtrack of American V8 muscle. That was serious firepower for a luxury coupe designed to transport its occupants in considerable comfort, especially when many performance cars were still struggling to combine refinement with outright speed. Buick also gave the Riviera GS mechanical upgrades worthy of its performance credentials. The Gran Sport package included a 3.42:1 Positraction rear axle, a freer-flowing dual exhaust system, and suspension improvements that sharpened handling. Power reached the rear wheels through a three-speed Super Turbine 400 automatic transmission featuring a variable-pitch torque converter. Despite weighing approximately 4,166 pounds, the Riviera GS could accelerate from 0-60 mph in around 7.2 seconds, impressive performance for a luxury coupe of its size and era. What made the 1965 Buick Riviera GS particularly interesting was its positioning within America's growing performance car landscape. The     Pontiac GTO and     Chevrolet Chevelle offered traditional muscle car excitement, while the Riviera went after people who wanted a powerful V8 wrapped in sophisticated styling. Its 117-inch wheelbase, distinctive bucket-seat interior, and relatively composed road manners made it a compelling American grand tourer. The rendering takes the Riviera's celebrated design and gives it the visual aggression of a much more modern muscle car. Up front, the famous vertical headlight arrangement remains recognizable, although modern LED lighting replaces the original concealed units. A substantial blacked-out grille dominates the nose, while a redesigned front bumper incorporates large lower air intakes and an aggressive splitter. The muscular front fenders retain their vintage character, creating an unusually convincing combination of '60s American luxury and plenty of modern touches. As for the profile, Buick's original long-hood, short-deck proportions remain beautifully preserved, but the restomod sits considerably closer to the pavement. Deep-dish alloy wheels fill the arches, accompanied by low-profile performance tires and a wider, more purposeful stance. The rich metallic burgundy paint changes character depending on the light, while the contrasting roof and carefully retained chrome trim maintain a connection to the original Riviera. At the back, horizontal LED taillights sit within a darkened rear panel, accompanied by prominent Buick lettering across the trunk lid. A redesigned rear bumper incorporates two large exhaust outlets, while the wide rear tires look pretty awesome and emphasize the car's personality. The original Riviera GS already had enough V8 torque to make its occupants appreciate the importance of comfortable seats. That said, a modern restomod project could take that performance considerably further. One possibility would involve retaining and upgrading the classic Nailhead V8, preserving the authentic character that makes the 1965 Buick Riviera GS special. Alternatively, a modern GM 6.2-liter V8 could provide the foundations for a considerably more powerful build, with 500 horsepower or more representing an achievable hypothetical target depending on the engine specification and modifications. Modernizing the drivetrain would also transform how this luxury muscle car behaves on American highways. A six-speed or 10-speed auto could improve acceleration, cruising refinement, and overall drivability compared with the original three-speed unit. Upgraded cooling, electronic fuel injection, and modern engine management would help support dependable performance. Given the Riviera's substantial weight and imposing dimensions, a properly engineered suspension setup and larger four-wheel disc brakes would be particularly important for those interested in enjoying their custom Buick beyond the occasional car show. Ultimately, this Buick Riviera GS restomod demonstrates how much untapped potential exists beyond America's usual muscle car favorites. Chevrolet Camaros, Pontiac GTOs, and classic Dodge Chargers have become familiar sights within the restomod world, but Buick's 1965 masterpiece is a relative virgin. Brilliant design, genuine V8 heritage, and luxury car sophistication means there's an excellent foundation for a sick custom build. If a talented American restomod specialist ever brings something resembling this rendering to life, Detroit's forgotten luxury muscle car could become one of the most desirable custom classics on the road.  moved into view today as large American banks edged toward the autumn earnings stretch, with trading desks, advisory pipelines and asset management units framing the market conversation across the financial sector. The firm, long regarded as a bellwether for Wall Street dealmaking, sits near the centre of a reporting calendar that tends to set the tone for the broad tape when the first wave of bank results lands. Attention across the sector has sharpened as the earnings window nears, and the bank's blend of capital markets muscle and a growing fee-based franchise keeps the name prominent in financial-sector commentary. The session reflected a market that remains attentive to how the largest American lenders describe trading conditions, deal flow and the lending backdrop heading into the colder months. The broad tape has stayed led by large-cap technology and semiconductors amid heavy spending on artificial-intelligence infrastructure, yet financials have quietly reclaimed a share of the spotlight as the reporting calendar fills out. Within that story, a franchise so closely tied to dealmaking and trading tends to be read as an early signal of where the sector is heading, which is part of why the name featured so prominently in the day's financial commentary. The company operates one of the most recognised franchises in global finance, spanning advisory work on mergers and acquisitions, underwriting of equity and debt issuance, and sprawling trading operations across fixed interest, currencies, commodities and equities. These capital markets arms have historically defined the brand and still account for a sizeable slice of the firm's revenue mix. Alongside the trading floors, the group runs an asset and wealth management division that oversees portfolios for institutions and affluent households, and a transaction banking effort that handles cash management and payments for corporate clients. The combination gives the franchise both the cyclicality of market-driven desks and the steadier cadence of fee-based mandates, a balance management has worked to tilt toward recurring revenue. That structure makes the firm unusually sensitive to the rhythm of financial markets themselves, rather than to the everyday banking of households. Where a retail-heavy lender leans on deposits and consumer credit, this franchise rises and falls with the appetite of corporations to raise money and strike deals, and with the willingness of institutions to trade. The distinction frames how the market interprets each quarter from the group. Advisory and underwriting fees sit at the heart of how the market reads this particular bank. When corporate confidence firms and boardrooms move ahead with mergers, acquisitions and new share sales, the advisory engine tends to hum, and the firm captures fees across the life of each transaction. A quieter stretch, by contrast, tends to weigh on the same lines. Commentary around the sector has pointed to a gradual thaw in dealmaking after a muted spell, with sponsors and corporates returning to the negotiating table. For a franchise weighted toward capital markets, the pace of that revival carries unusual weight, and market watchers track the pipeline of announced transactions as a read on the months ahead for the advisory desks. The underwriting side mirrors that pattern. A reopening of the market for new share listings and a steady flow of corporate debt issuance both feed the fee lines that this franchise depends upon, and a thaw in either channel tends to brighten the tone around the name. The breadth of the pipeline, rather than any single mandate, is what the market watches as a gauge of momentum into the reporting stretch. Trading revenue remains a defining feature of the group, and the equities and fixed interest desks can swing meaningfully with market volatility, client flow and the mix of products changing hands. Busy, choppy markets often favour the trading floors, as clients reposition and hedge, while becalmed conditions tend to thin the activity that generates desk revenue. The recent tape, led by large-cap technology and semiconductors amid heavy spending on artificial-intelligence infrastructure, has produced bursts of activity across equities and rates. How those flows translated into desk performance over the quarter is among the most watched questions as the reporting stretch nears, given how central trading remains to the overall revenue picture. Because trading can lurch from quarter to quarter, the market tends to read a single strong or soft stretch cautiously, looking instead at how the desks perform across a run of periods. Consistency, rather than a one-off spike, is what tends to reassure observers that the trading engine is firing in a durable way, and that framing shapes the questions raised around the name as results approach. The session unfolded against a market that has kept large American banks firmly in focus heading into the earnings stretch. Financial shares have drawn renewed attention as the sector prepares to describe lending conditions, deposit trends and capital markets momentum, and the tone set by the earliest reporters often colours sentiment across the group. The sequencing of the calendar matters as well. Because a handful of the largest banks report within days of one another, early results tend to frame how the market reads those that follow, turning the opening days of the stretch into a reference point for the whole sector. For readers tracking the broad sweep of lenders, brokers and asset managers that make up the sector, a wider reading sits with US Financial Stocks, where the themes shaping banks, trading houses and wealth franchises are followed as a connected whole rather than one name at a time. The path of interest rates shapes almost every corner of a large bank, and Goldman is no exception. Movements at the Federal Reserve ripple through lending margins, the cost of deposits, the appetite for fresh borrowing and the pricing of trading books, making the central bank's rate decisions a recurring theme in sector discussion. Market participants have watched the rate debate closely, weighing how the balance between cooling price pressures and a resilient American economy might steer the central bank's next moves. For a franchise that both lends and trades across rate-sensitive markets, the direction of that debate feeds directly into how the desks and the balance sheet are discussed through the reporting stretch. A clearer rate backdrop also tends to encourage the corporate activity that drives advisory and underwriting. When borrowing costs settle into a steadier range, boardrooms find it easier to price deals and commit to transactions, which is why the rate conversation reaches well beyond the lending book and into the fee engines at the heart of this particular franchise. The asset and wealth management arm has become a larger part of the story as management has pushed to lift the share of revenue that recurs regardless of the trading cycle. Managing money for institutions and wealthy families generates steadier fees, and the unit has been framed as a stabiliser against the swings of the capital markets desks. Growth in assets under supervision, the flow of new mandates and the mix between higher-fee and lower-fee products all feed into how this division is read. A steadier fee base can soften the quarter-to-quarter lurches that come with heavy reliance on trading, and the progress of that shift remains a closely followed strand of the broader narrative. The push into private markets strategies has added another dimension, as the firm seeks to manage capital across credit, real assets and private equity alongside its traditional franchises. These mandates tend to carry longer lifespans and steadier fees than the trading desks, reinforcing the recurring-revenue character that management has sought to build across the wider group. Capital remains a defining topic for the largest American banks, which operate under demanding regulatory standards that govern how much of a buffer each firm must carry. The strength of that buffer influences how freely a bank can fund dividends and share buybacks, and the subject tends to resurface whenever regulators update their stress-test frameworks. For Goldman, the balance between retaining capital to support the business and distributing it back to owners sits within those rules. The firm's standing on this front is watched as a measure of resilience, and commentary around the sector regularly circles back to how comfortably the big banks sit above their required thresholds as conditions shift. The stress-test regime itself has been a recurring talking point, as the thresholds that govern the buffers can move from one cycle to the next. How a capital-markets-heavy firm fares under the scenarios regulators design, which often stress trading books severely, feeds into how the market gauges the headroom available to fund dividends and buybacks across the group. The competitive field is crowded and fierce. Goldman contends with the other large American universal banks across advisory and trading, with specialist boutiques that compete for marquee advisory assignments, and with an expanding set of private capital firms that increasingly fund deals outside the traditional banking channel. That rivalry keeps pressure on fees and on the war for senior talent, the bankers and traders whose client relationships drive revenue. The firm's standing in league tables, its ability to retain top dealmakers and its reach across regions all factor into how the market measures the franchise against a demanding set of peers. The rise of private capital has reshaped the landscape in particular, as large pools of money now sit outside the banks and compete to finance the very transactions the advisory desks once dominated. How the firm positions itself alongside, rather than purely against, those pools has become a strategic thread that the market follows closely as the sector evolves. Strategic direction has been a running theme, with management stepping back from an earlier push into mainstream consumer banking to refocus on the areas where the firm has long carried an edge. The pivot back toward advisory, trading and asset and wealth management has been described as a sharpening of the core, trimming ventures that strayed from the historic strengths. That recalibration shapes how the market frames the group's direction, as the emphasis swings back to the institutional and affluent client base the brand was built around. The pace and discipline of the realignment feed into sector commentary, with observers tracking how cleanly the firm narrows its focus to the franchises it knows best. Winding down a consumer effort is rarely instant, and the market has tracked how smoothly the firm sheds the pieces that no longer fit while limiting any drag on the core. A cleaner, more focused franchise is the stated aim, and the discipline of that unwinding is read as a measure of how firmly management can execute a strategic turn. The firm's reach spans the major financial centres, from New York and London to the fast-growing hubs of Asia, giving it a seat at the table on cross-border transactions that smaller rivals cannot match. That global footprint shapes how the market reads the franchise, since a slowdown in one region can be offset by activity in another. Cross-border dealmaking tends to favour the banks that can field teams across continents, and a presence in multiple centres lets the firm follow its clients wherever a transaction leads. The breadth of that network is read as a durable edge, particularly as corporations weigh expansion and consolidation across borders. Currency swings and differing regional conditions add complexity to a global franchise, yet they also create the very flows that keep the trading desks busy. How the firm navigates the patchwork of regional environments, from the pace of European dealmaking to the rhythm of Asian markets, feeds into how the overall picture is assessed through the reporting stretch. Few financial names carry the symbolic weight of this one when markets turn their eyes to Wall Street earnings. As a franchise tilted toward capital markets, its results are read not only as a measure of a single company but as a signal about dealmaking appetite, trading conditions and the health of the broader financial engine. That is why the stock stays prominent as the reporting stretch nears. The session placed Goldman within a sector-wide story in which the largest American banks prepare to describe the environment they have navigated, and the firm's capital markets lean makes its contribution to that story one of the most closely parsed across the financial tape. For the market, then, the name serves as both a company and a gauge. The questions that surround it, from the pace of dealmaking to the firmness of trading and the steadiness of the wealth engine, are the same questions the broader financial sector faces as autumn gives way to the reporting season, which keeps the franchise squarely in the frame. title: Wedmont Private Capital Grows Position in The Goldman Sachs Group, Inc. $GS - MarketBeat

Wedmont Private Capital raised its holdings in shares of The Goldman Sachs Group, Inc. The institutional investor owned 7,523 shares of the investment management company's stock after acquiring an additional 1,581 shares during the quarter. Wedmont Private Capital's holdings in The Goldman Sachs Group were worth $6,640,000 at the end of the most recent reporting period. Other hedge funds and other institutional investors also recently made changes to their positions in the company. Intelligence Driven Advisers LLC boosted its stake in shares of The Goldman Sachs Group by 38.9% during the 3rd quarter. title: The 10 Best Motorcycles You Can Buy In 2026 And 2027 - Top Speed
content: Subscribe to the TopSpeed newsletter to never miss an update There isn't really one best motorcycle for everyone. A first-time rider shopping for a lightweight commuter has almost nothing in common with someone planning a cross-country adventure, while the person eyeing an electric motorcycle may not care about either. So instead of pretending one machine can win every argument, we've picked 10 of the strongest motorcycles available in the U.S. for 2026 and 2027, split across five very different categories. Our picks cover beginner bikes, cruisers, adventure motorcycles, sport bikes, and electric machines. Each one brings something particularly compelling to its corner of the market, whether that's price, accessibility, performance, technology, or simply a combination that's difficult for its rivals to match. The Kawasaki Ninja 500 is one of the easiest answers to the best beginner motorcycle question because it doesn't require much compromise once you've learned the basics. Its 451cc parallel-twin produces a claimed 51 horsepower at 10,000 rpm and 31.7 pound-feet at 7,500 rpm, paired with a six-speed transmission. The ABS version weighs just over 377 pounds in 50-state specification, while its 30.9-inch seat keeps things approachable for newer riders. It's also inexpensive enough to make sense as a first bike. The 2026 Ninja 500 starts at $5,399 without ABS, while ABS-equipped models begin at $5,799. A 3.7-gallon tank, smartphone-connected instrumentation, sporty bodywork, and a chassis light enough for city riding give it considerably more versatility than the "starter bike" label suggests. You could learn on one, commute on it, spend weekends carving corners, and keep it long after gaining full confidence. 51 horsepower @ 10,000 rpm; 31.7 pound-feet @ 7,500 rpm Single 310mm front disc, two-piston caliper; 220mm rear disc, single-piston caliper; ABS optional 372.6 pounds non-ABS / 377.1 pounds ABS, 50-state specification Available ABS, smartphone connectivity, LCD instrumentation, economical riding indicator For riders who want their best starter motorcycle to be even lighter and less intimidating, the 2026 Yamaha MT-03 makes a persuasive case. Its 321cc liquid-cooled parallel-twin feeds a six-speed gearbox with an assist-and-slipper clutch, while the whole motorcycle weighs 373 pounds ready to ride. The 30.7-inch seat height is equally welcoming, particularly for shorter riders who would rather have both feet confidently near the pavement while learning low-speed control.​​​​​​​ The MT-03 starts at just $4,999 and uses a 37mm inverted KYB fork, preload-adjustable rear shock, ABS, and 17-inch wheels at both ends. Yamaha also updated the current model with revised styling and smartphone connectivity. It isn't overwhelmingly fast, and that is part of the appeal. For someone searching for the best motorcycle for beginners who'll primarily ride around town and on back roads, simplicity can be far more useful than another 30 horsepower. 42 horsepower @ 10,750 RPM and 21.8 to 22 lb-ft of torque @ 9,000 RPM Six-speed; assist-and-slipper wet multiplate clutch; chain drive ABS, Y-Connect smartphone connectivity, LCD display, LED lighting, USB-A outlet The 2026 Honda Rebel 1100 earns a spot on our best cruiser motorcycle shortlist because it bridges the gap between an approachable middleweight and a genuinely quick big-bore cruiser. Its 1,084cc liquid-cooled parallel-twin is paired with a conventional six-speed manual on the $9,699 base model, while Honda continues to offer its automatic dual-clutch transmission on higher trims. A 27.9-inch seat keeps the riding position accessible despite the substantial engine sitting underneath you. The standard Rebel weighs 497 pounds ready to ride, which is relatively manageable by large-cruiser standards. It gets a 43mm fork with 5.5 inches of travel, dual preload-adjustable Showa shocks, ABS, and a 330mm front brake. The result is a cruiser that can handle urban riding, highways, and winding roads without adopting the enormous dimensions of a traditional heavyweight. Buyers wanting even easier cruising can step up to the 519-pound DCT version. 87.2 horsepower @ 7,250 rpm; 72.3 pound-feet @ 4,750 rpm, claimed internationally Single 330mm front disc with radial-mount four-piston caliper; single 256mm rear disc; ABS 18-inch front / 16-inch rear; 130/70-18 front, 180/65-16 rear ABS, selectable ride modes, traction control, wheelie control, cruise control, throttle-by-wire, RoadSync smartphone connectivity If you want your cruiser to look and sound considerably more traditional, the Indian Scout Bobber brings a proper American V-twin into the equation. Its liquid-cooled 1,250cc 60-degree V-twin produces 105 horsepower and 82 pound-feet of torque, driving through a six-speed transmission. Indian wraps all of that in a low-slung chassis with chopped fenders, chunky 16-inch wheels, blacked-out finishes, and an extremely low 25.6-inch laden seat height. It isn't light at 542 pounds in running order, but that's still sensible territory for a full-size American cruiser. A 41mm fork, dual rear shocks, Pirelli MT60RS tires, and single 298mm brake discs front and rear keep the hardware straightforward. Pricing starts at $12,999, with more feature-heavy trims available above it. The Scout Bobber earns its spot because it delivers the visual drama people expect from a cruiser without relying on a gigantic air-cooled engine or 700-pound curb weight. Single 298mm front disc with two-piston caliper; single 298mm rear disc with one-piston caliper 16-inch cast wheels; Pirelli MT60RS 130/90B16 front, 150/80B16 rear ABS, LED lighting, digital instrumentation; additional electronic features available on higher trims BMW's 2027 F 450 GS may be new, but on paper it already looks like one of the strongest contenders for the best adventure motorcycle title in the lightweight class. Its new 420cc parallel-twin produces 48 horsepower at 8,750 rpm and 32 pound-feet at 6,750 rpm. More importantly, the bike weighs just 393 pounds road-ready, has a 33.3-inch seat, and provides 7.1 inches of suspension travel at both ends. U.S. pricing starts at a very competitive $6,995. BMW hasn't stripped the little GS bare to hit that price, either. ABS, traction control, multiple ride modes, heated grips, a 6.5-inch TFT display, USB-C charging, a skid plate, and adjustable controls come standard. Sport and GS Trophy versions add more off-road-focused equipment, while BMW's Easy Ride centrifugal clutch appears on higher specifications. U.S. deliveries are expected in the first quarter of 2027, making this the newest motorcycle on our list. 420cc liquid-cooled DOHC parallel-twin with 135-degree crankshaft offset 48 horsepower @ 8,750 rpm; 32 pound-feet @ 6,750 rpm Six-speed; hydraulically operated wet multi-disc clutch; chain drive Single 310mm front disc with four-piston Brembo monobloc caliper; 240mm rear disc; cornering ABS 19-inch front / 17-inch rear; 100/90-19 front, 130/80-17 rear Cornering ABS, traction control, engine-brake control, Dynamic Brake Control, Rain/Road/Enduro modes, 6.5-inch TFT, connectivity, heated grips The 2026 Yamaha Ténéré 700 approaches adventure riding from the opposite direction. Instead of loading the bike with every electronic feature imaginable, Yamaha built it around the proven 689cc CP2 parallel-twin and a chassis meant to tolerate actual dirt. The current U.S. model weighs 459 pounds wet, offers 9.4 inches of ground clearance, and rides on proper 21-inch front and 18-inch rear wheels wrapped in Pirelli Scorpion Rally STR tires. Its fully adjustable 43mm inverted fork provides 8.3 inches of travel, while the rear gets 7.9 inches and remote preload adjustment. Selectable ABS lets riders tailor the bike for off-road use, while the 4.2-gallon tank and comfortable upright ergonomics keep it viable for longer trips. At $10,999, the Ténéré isn't the cheapest middleweight ADV anymore, but its relatively straightforward formula remains one of the category's most convincing combinations of road manners and genuine trail capability. 72.4 horsepower @ 9,000 rpm; 50.2 pound-feet @ 6,500 rpm, claimed internationally Dual 282mm front discs; single 245mm rear disc; three-mode selectable ABS 21-inch front / 18-inch rear; Pirelli Scorpion Rally STR 90/90R21 front, 150/70R18 rear Ride-by-wire, Sport and Explorer throttle maps, three-mode selectable ABS, 6.3-inch TFT, smartphone connectivity and navigation The Yamaha YZF-R9 fills the gap between lightweight twins and intimidating liter-class superbikes. Its 890cc CP3 inline-three feeds a six-speed transmission and sits inside a purpose-built aluminum chassis, giving Yamaha's familiar triple a much sharper home than the MT-09 platform. At 430 pounds wet with a 32.7-inch seat, the R9 offers serious performance without becoming a 200-horsepower missile that needs a racetrack before its engine starts making sense. The hardware backs up the intent. Yamaha gives it a fully adjustable 43mm KYB fork and similarly adjustable rear shock, dual 320mm front brakes, 17-inch wheels, and a comprehensive electronics package. MSRP starts at $12,499, putting the R9 in an interesting middle ground between everyday sport bikes and flagship superbikes. For road riders who still want legitimate track capability, it may be one of the most rational high-performance motorcycles available today. 117.4 horsepower @ 10,000 rpm; 68.6 pound-feet @ 7,000 rpm, claimed internationally Six-speed; assist-and-slipper wet clutch; up/down quickshifter Dual 320mm front discs with Brembo Stylema calipers; 220mm rear disc; ABS 17-inch wheels; Bridgestone Battlax Hypersport S22 120/70ZR17 front, 180/55ZR17 rear Six-axis IMU-based rider aids, ride modes, traction control, slide control, lift control, brake control, launch control, engine-brake management, quickshifter, cruise control and speed limiter Ducati's latest Panigale V2 demonstrates that a modern sport bike doesn't need superbike horsepower to be properly exotic. Its 890cc 90-degree V-twin produces 120 horsepower, uses variable intake valve timing, and sends power through a six-speed gearbox with a standard up-and-down quickshifter. The new engine is dramatically lighter than Ducati's previous twin, helping make this generation of Panigale V2 significantly less cumbersome than the 955cc machine it replaced. The chassis uses an aluminum monocoque with the engine as a structural component, while a fully adjustable 43mm Marzocchi fork handles the front end on the standard model. Electronics include cornering ABS, traction control, wheelie control, engine-braking management, and multiple riding modes. Current U.S. pricing for the 2026 Panigale V2 is $16,995. It's still unmistakably a Ducati superbike, just one whose performance is far easier to exploit away from a professional race circuit. 890cc liquid-cooled 90-degree V-twin with variable intake valve timing 120 horsepower @ 10,750 rpm; 69 pound-feet @ 8,250 rpm Six-speed; slipper wet clutch; up/down quickshifter Dual 320mm front discs with Brembo M50 four-piston monobloc calipers; 245mm rear disc; cornering ABS 17-inch aluminum wheels; Pirelli Diablo Rosso IV 120/70 ZR17 front, 190/55 ZR17 rear Cornering ABS, traction control, wheelie control, engine-brake control, ride modes, power modes, quickshifter, 5-inch TFT The Zero SR/F remains one of the clearest answers to the best electric motorcycle question if your priorities are outright performance and useful road range. Its Z-Force motor produces 111 horsepower and a massive 140 pound-feet of torque, while the 17.3-kWh battery delivers a claimed city range of up to 176 miles. Top speed is 124 miles per hour, which puts the SR/F firmly in full-size performance motorcycle territory rather than positioning it as an electrified urban runabout. Pricing starts at $19,995, so the SR/F certainly isn't cheap, but it offers considerably more performance and range than entry-level electric machines. Zero also offers an optional Power Tank and 6-kW Rapid Charger for riders who want to extend its capabilities further. It is the choice here for someone who wants electric propulsion without abandoning the speed, chassis proportions, and highway capability associated with a conventional large motorcycle.​​​​​​​ Z-Force 75-10 air-cooled interior permanent-magnet AC electric motor; 17.3-kWh battery Dual 320mm front discs with J.Juan radial four-piston calipers; 240mm rear disc; Bosch stability control 17-inch wheels; Pirelli Diablo Rosso III 120/70-17 front, 180/55-17 rear Bosch Motorcycle Stability Control, cornering ABS, traction control, drag-torque control, multiple ride modes, Cypher III+ operating system, cruise control and connected TFT The LiveWire S2 Alpinista takes a different approach to electric performance. Its motor produces 84 horsepower and an enormous 194 pound-feet of torque, enough for a claimed zero-to-60-miles-per-hour run in three seconds. Top speed is 99 miles per hour, while estimated city range reaches 120 miles. The Alpinista also rolls on 17-inch wheels front and rear, giving it a more conventional sport-standard setup than the flat-track-inspired S2 Del Mar. Perhaps the biggest improvement is the price. LiveWire has cut the Alpinista to $12,999, making the S2 platform far easier to justify than when the company's electric motorcycles sat closer to premium superbike money. Level 1 and Level 2 charging are supported, with LiveWire quoting 78 minutes for a Level 2 charge under its specified conditions. For riders whose mileage is mostly urban and suburban, the Alpinista makes a strong case that electric motorcycles can already be genuinely entertaining everyday machines. title: The Middleweight ADV Bike With BMW GS Comfort And Italian Character - Top Speed
content: Subscribe to the TopSpeed newsletter to never miss an update BMW’s GS lineup has dominated the adventure bike segment (be it midweight or full-size) for a long time now. But that also means these machines are rather common today. So it’s fair for you–as a potential ADV customer–to want something different but with similar comfort and pizazz as the GS. If that sums up your ADV dilemma right now, we have a solution. It hails from Italy (actually made in Italy, unlike certain Ducatis), has a boxer-like powerhouse, and tops all that with top-drawer comfort for the midweight space. Speaking of today’s midweight space, nearly every bikemaker has entered the party. Some take a really serious approach, like the KTM 890 Adventure R. These are off-road-centric machines first, with a focus on comfort coming as a secondary or tertiary requirement. The Tiger 900 Rally Pro belongs in the same space. Opposite to them are road-biased machines like the Triumph Tiger 850 Sport and Suzuki V-Strom 800 (non-DE). They want to stay on the road as much as possible, although the 19-inch wheel does allow an occasional excursion. All that means there is something for everyone here, whatever your requirements may be. However, things narrow down drastically as soon as you bring Italian character into the mix. You’re technically left with just four or five bikes. Two of these come from Ducati: the fresh DesertX V2 and the Multistrada V2. The former takes the off-road-centric approach, while the latter takes the road-biased approach. So neither has the BMW GS balance we’re looking for. Same goes for the Aprilia Tuareg 660. That leaves us with an off-beat Italian machine from Moto Guzzi, which has the best blend of Italian character and BMW comfort. We’re talking about the V85 TT. This is Moto Guzzi’s answer for the new-age middleweight ADV class, taking on motorcycles from all over the world. Its arch-rival, though, seems to be BMW’s F 800 GS. And the TT does a great job at matching it in some regards, while beating it in others. At the same time, its Italian nature means you get that exclusive swagger you’d expect from a premium brand. Not to mention, Moto Guzzi remains lesser-known in the US, so you’ll surely have people striking up conversations at bike meets. Speaking of which, the V85 is offered in three trims. The Strada serves as the stripped-back base variant, mainly focused toward road riding first evident from the alloy wheels. Then, we have the TT that brings spoke wheels and a couple of other extras for a more ADV-like experience. Last but not least is the touring-ready Travel version. This builds on the TT by throwing in a larger windscreen, hard panniers, heated grips, and a special livery. Out of these, the TT is the most complete, which is why we’re focusing on that here. The V85 TT sells for $12,790. That positions it right in the heat of the midweight ADV segment, above smaller bikes like the Yamaha Tenere 700 and Suzuki V-Strom 800DE, but below more premium bikes like the KTM 890 Super Adventure R and BMW F 900 GS. More importantly, it sits $1,795 more expensive than the base F 800 GS. That isn’t a nice place to be since underrated bikes usually need to undercut direct rivals to stand out in the segment. You should know that the V85’s case gets better once you dive into the details. On that note, the most unique aspect here is arguably the engine. You get a transversal air-cooled 853cc V-twin powerhouse, setting it apart from the sea of parallel-twin rivals. So the cylinders protrude outward from the chassis for a distinct aesthetic. As for output, you get 80 horsepower and 61 pound-feet, with the latter at just 5,100 RPM. That is lower than nearly all of its midweight rivals. You also get variable valve timing for an even better spread of power. All that juice reaches the wheel via a six-speed transmission and final shaft drive. The latter means no worry of chain cleaning every 300 miles. Coming to the chassis, Moto Guzzi has made sure the V85 ticks the essential boxes. A steel trellis chassis is present as the centerpiece, housed on 41 mm USD forks and a monoshock. The shock is laterally mounted instead of in a central position like rivals. While we don’t know the advantage of this, we do know there is 6.7 inches of travel and adjustability at both ends. You even get a remote preload adjuster at the rear–a rarity in this price bracket. Rounding things off are the wheels and brakes. A set of 19/17-inch cross-spoke wheels come standard, featuring dual 320 mm front discs with Brembo monobloc four-piston calipers and a 260 mm rear disc with a two-piston caliper. Overall, the package seems enough for gliding over most stuff you’ll encounter in the real world or on occasional trails. While at it, you’ll appreciate the likable dimensions. The saddle height is 32.6 inches, while the weight is 507 pounds. Considering you get one of the largest fuel tanks (six gallons) in the midweight segment, the weight is impressively low. However, Moto Guzzi hasn’t shed light on the wheelbase, ground clearance, or rake. No Italian bikemaker holds back on tech in 2026, and Moto Guzzi isn’t different. A six-axis IMU and ride-by-wire work in tandem to allow cornering ABS, traction control, ride modes, and cruise control. You access these via a TFT instrument cluster–identical to some Aprilias–that shows a variety of information and has smartphone connectivity for tracking phone info on the fly. Lastly, nitty-gritty bits like LED lights, an adjustable windscreen, an aluminum skid plate, and handguards boost the attention to detail. We want to hear from you. title: Hedge Funds Are Cautious on Stocks amid Rates and Energy Volatility - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. Hedge fund positioning in equities for long-short strategies is at historically low levels amid ongoing volatility in interest rates and oil prices, says Mark Wilson, head of European Equity Franchise Sales and Hedge Fund Coverage in Goldman Sachs FICC and Equities. And even as investor scrutiny of French government borrowing grows, Wilson points out that there are investment opportunities in Europe in defense stocks and the energy independence theme. In The Markets podcast, he also discusses his outlook for mega-capitalization technology companies, stocks that benefit from German government spending, and US third-quarter earnings. Chris Hussey: This is The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey, and today is Wednesday, October 7th, and I'm here in the Goldman Sachs trading floor with Mark Wilson, who is head of European Equities, Franchise Sales and Hedge Fund Coverage within our FICC and Equities Group. Mark, thanks so much for joining us. Chris Hussey: Okay, Mark always great to have you here. Let's kick it off with the two headwinds in the market today. Rates have been going higher, oil's been going higher. Europe, of course, is exposed to both. What is Europe exposed to most, and what are clients caring about most here? Mark Wilson: In Europe, we are more vulnerable to the energy shock, and so the inflationary pressure is higher. If you think about the feed through to the markets, on six-month correlations, Euro stocks and 10-year Bund yields are about negative 70% correlated right now. You haven't seen that degree of negative correlation since back to the 1990s, so this is really a bit of a regime shift. You're right to ask the question though, because obviously over the last couple of weeks we've had a much more idiosyncratic event in Europe. OAT spreads versus Bunds have blown out, and some of the social, but mainly political issues focused around the upcoming budget in France have been a real problem. And so that's a major European specific issue, which is now there, and I think will be an ongoing feature over the next few months as we get towards the presidential elections in France in the first half of next year. Ultimately, here and now, the two things which clients are most focused on are the price behavior of that OAT-Bund spread, and also the energy and gas inventory stock situation as we head in towards winter. Chris Hussey: Okay, Mark, I get it. Oil more important than rates in Europe, but we also know that rates matter a lot to stocks. What are you seeing from clients around how rates are impacting stock valuation and positioning? Mark Wilson: In terms of equities specifically, and this isn't just common to Europe, you've seen a very logical de-rating in equity markets. So, S&P multiple has come down, same is true in Europe. If you look at the more rate sensitive parts of the market, if you look at European renewables, for example, they've de-rated at well over 20%, and so you've seen this quite logical re-rating, de-rating specifically, in equities in response to higher rates. You mentioned positioning. I think the most standout piece of information that we've been thinking about the last couple of weeks is just how much this has caused investors to reappraise their equity exposure and their equity risk. So, to put a number on this, we look at our fundamental hedge funds and their net exposure to the markets, and if you look at US-specific fundamental long-short clients today, their net length is in the north percentile on a one-year look-back. It's at a two and three percentile on a three-year and five-year look-back. I think globally, global fundamental long shorts, these are anywhere from nought to 9% in terms of their net length and exposure to the market. So positioning has been really cut in response to rates and a bunch of other uncertainties that are out there. Chris Hussey: Yeah. That, that is, that is a fascinating number, and nought, for our audience, is zero in England. So, let me expand, though, onto your energy comment, cause you make an interesting energy comment around how Europe is so exposed here. What many people don't realize is nat gas is the exposure as much as oil, and there have been, our commodities team has written about the potential for nat gas to really spike maybe five, ten times what you have to pay for nat gas in the US. Are you seeing that in the industrial complex of Europe yet? Are you seeing these in the numbers, or is this just something people are scared about and it's not something in the numbers yet? Mark Wilson: So it is in the numbers. Europe has definite competitive issues related to higher energy price costs, but this isn't new news. Europe trades cheaper. Part of it is this phenomena. These competitive threats are impacting industry and impacting the market. I do think, though, the starting point matters, and Europe is a lot cheaper than other global markets, especially the US, and so some of that is already in the price, and I don't think it's an impediment to performance. European banks have beaten Mag Seven on a one-year, three-year, four-year look-back, and so there's the opportunity for performance, but it's certainly a competitive headwind and issue for Europe. Chris Hussey: All right, Mark. 25 years ago, you were brokering me as a US analyst in Europe, so I know you know the US markets well. I know now -- Chris Hussey: Well, I know that you now know the European markets really well. So, I want you to compare US versus Europe here. Talk to me. Is Europe a value trap here with all the headwinds that they're facing, or is Europe an opportunity because it's so cheap? Mark Wilson: So part of the European discount is certainly because of the index composition. We have less tech, we have less high-growth companies, and so inevitably there is a value element to it. The European market has been holding its own. I mean, it's kept up with the US this year, and part of that is because there are some clear investment cycles within Europe, within industrials, within renewables, within defense. And what I'd say is the last few years have had a series of ongoing challenges to Europe, and Europe is slow to respond, but Europe is responding. So when you go back to COVID, there was a very large fiscal mobilization. Pretty soon afterwards, you had the Russia-Ukraine conflict and a real acknowledgment of a need for energy independence domestically. Not long after that, you had the challenge of the Iranian conflict and the obvious heightened energy issues, and the AI cycle in of itself is a challenge to Europe to respond, to have its own deployment. And so, within Europe, these forcing mechanisms have continued to compound and to drive action and to drive response. And so what I'd say is there are real themes to invest behind. That industrial theme, the rearmament of Europe, the drive for energy independence. And demographics has been one of the key issues for Europe and one of the key bear theses and one of the key planks of this value trap argument. This argument around demographics is destiny, I think, is somewhat being debunked when we think about the real power of AI and the deployment of AI, which will be very prevalent soon. Demographics times agents deployed in the economy could be a real uplift to demographically challenged areas. And so I think there's increasing hope that actually the European market offers real opportunity, and as the strategy to respond to these challenges becomes more evident. Chris Hussey: Okay. Third quarter earnings season is right upon us. We're going to kick it off in the United States tomorrow. Europe and the US, and the world more generally, is this peak earnings, or is this another opportunity to buy the earnings growth? Mark Wilson: So, I'm pretty sure in the US we have peak earnings growth for the third quarter. I think 27% earnings growth in the US, which is topping an amazing run in terms of earnings growth. And that's a clean earnings number, not taking benefit for all these one-time gains. Europe has actually been similarly strong, so we're forecasting 22% earnings growth year on year for the second half of this year. It's aided a little bit by the energy benefit, so there's a big composition within the index of energy companies. Clean of the energy stocks, we're still looking at 15% earnings growth. So yes, I think the second derivative is slowing, especially in the US, but the earnings growth environment speaks to that high nominal growth environment that we spoke about at the beginning. And given that we're now transitioning, about to transition into a new calendar year, and you've seen this very significant multiple compression, I do think where you see high nominal growth, where you see high corporate earnings and a more reasonable multiple, the market setup is still pretty favorable. Chris Hussey: All right, Mark, let's put a bow on it. What's the trade? Mark Wilson: The first one is US-focused. There's been a lot of commentary around the narrowness of the US market performance, and the largest stocks in the index have been the largest spenders. There's been a huge amount of focus on the ROIC and the returns in which these spenders may garner, and I think that the momentum around real AI adoption is beginning to come through, whether it's Muse and other products in the consumer hands, or whether it's some of the enterprise adoption that we're beginning to see, the numbers are clear. And I do think that some of the hyperscaler revenue growth is really lagging by three, four, five, six quarters, the very strong CapEx spend north of 100% that we're seeing, the very, very strong cloud revenue backlog that we're seeing, again, north of 100%. And so, I think as we begin to see some of this ROIC and the real return on spend come through, I absolutely want to be long US mega cap tech. The second one is German fiscal spend beneficiaries. We know how strong the US growth story has been. German manufacturing PMIs are actually outpacing the US right now. Part of that is because as the rest of the world worries about fiscal space, the Germans are able to fiscally expand, and that's driving significant investment across broad industrial complex in Germany. Through this year, you've seen 13 to 14% estimates revisions for EPS, yet those stocks have derated over 20% as well. So right now you're paying low teens multiple for a group of companies that is going to grow earnings in line with the US market over the next 12 and 24 months, so I want to be long that basket of German fiscal spend beneficiaries. Chris Hussey: I love it. US mega cap tech, the harvesters, and the German fiscal beneficiaries. Great. Okay, Mark, last question. What are you watching for next week? Mark Wilson: So, first order I think is going to be CPI next Wednesday. It's going to be all important when we think about what might break this trend of, higher yields. Good news on the inflation front is going to be key. I do think there's a window of opportunity for some news and a break in the Iran conflict given the timing now ahead of the midterms. And then I think all importantly, you mentioned it before, we're going to go into third quarter earnings. We've been in this unique period where really the micro is driving the macro, and I think as we learn more about the state of the AI trade as we go through corporate earnings, that's going to be all important. Chris Hussey: Mark Wilson, you are always a wealth of information. Thanks so much for joining us. Chris Hussey: That does it for this week's episode of The Markets. I'm Chris Hussey. Thanks for listening. title: Why US Consumers Are Downbeat Despite a Healthy Economy - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. Cost-of-living pressures are weighing on US households. However, the downbeat sentiment about the economy among Americans is so widespread that it suggests something else may also be at work, explains Joseph Briggs, who leads the Global Economics team within Goldman Sachs Research. He says the reason may be a broad decline in trust in US institutions. Data show a significant gap between consumer surveys and the sentiment levels that economic models would predict. This suggests that current sentiment survey readings “probably won’t be a very useful tool for economic analysis,” Briggs says. Joseph Briggs: Americans feel worse about the economy than the numbers suggest they should. The question is why? If we look at the consumer sentiment level we’d expect given the fundamentals – a healthy labor market, solid consumer spending, GDP growth – and then the actual average sentiment level, there’s quite a gap. Some of the reasons are intuitive. Cost-of-living pressures, where are most acutely felt by lower-income households, are a main one. But what's striking is that since 2019, just about every group has become more negative on the economy. Whether you look at wealth, income, age, political party, or even social media use, sentiment is down. Americans have become more downbeat overall surveys show. And that in turn is increasingly correlated in declining confidence in institutions. Over the last ten years, almost all of them have seen a drop from science to education, to medicine. So, the final question we ask is what weights more on Americans’ happiness: their level of financial satisfaction or their lack of confidence in institutions? And our analysis shows it’s much more a fundamental, downbeat view on institutions and the state of the world. So as long as consumer sentiment doesn’t really reflect sentiment about the economy, well, it probably won’t be a very useful tool for economic analysis. title: Trilla G’s spotlights new wave of Bouyon acts - St Vincent Times
content: Dominican artist Trilla-G (Gael Jno. Baptiste) through his Still Trill Entertainment is shining a spotlight on the island’s emerging Bouyon talents with the launch of the “Up Next Cypher,” a platform designed to give the next generation of Dominican artists an opportunity to be heard, seen and celebrated. Vol. 1 features G’z Up (Phillip Martin), Don Lash (Cadeem McPherson), Pa Pel (Loic Arius), Avatar Omish (Omari Dayl James), Ras B (Bayna Bellot) and Pryhmex (Ajahlie Ettienne), alongside Trilla himself.  The cypher gives each artist a chance to step up to the mic, represent and let listeners know exactly what they are bringing to the table. Produced by Shane Massicott of Kwib La Beats and mixed and mastered by ThaWizZarD (Cecil Joseph Jr.), the track puts everyone on one beat- the classic cypher format, where artists take turns showing off their talent and unique personalities. The concept had been on Trilla-G’s mind for some time. On Saturday 28 September 2026, the idea turned into reality, as he brought together several young artists who had previously approached him about collaborating or using his platform to showcase their talents. “I always wanted to do a Bouyon cypher,” Trilla-G explained. “Most of the guys you see in the video had already reached out to me at some point about working together or getting a chance to showcase their talent. Since I already had the idea of doing a cypher and wanted to put multiple people on, it just made sense.” The “Up Next Cypher” is an opportunity to introduce new voices to audiences and encourage emerging artists to take advantage of every platform available to them. The video, which is already generating significant attention across social media, was shot at The Lot Bar and Grill by Shane St. Claire of Sois Génial Multimedia and directed by Trilla-G and his Manager and creative collaborator Tridel “Wins” Edwin. Viewers have been weighing in on the artists, their performances and more importantly the future of Bouyon genre itself. The response has been stronger than Trilla-G anticipated “Honestly, the response has exceeded my expectations,” he said. “When I did it, I just wanted people to pay attention to the artists and show them some love, but the response has been overwhelming.” Trilla-G intends to continue developing the concept with more volumes to come and more talents to be introduced. “Right now, I just want to continue it and try to grow it as much as possible — continue introducing new talent,” he said. He is also encouraging the featured artists to make the most of the exposure and says he will continue doing what he can to work with emerging talents. The “Up Next Cypher” comes on the heels of a successful New York Labor Day weekend show for Trilla-G, who continues to expand his footprint and brand around the globe. He now invites fans to get ready for his best performance yet- on Saturday 24 October, at Dominica’s World Creole Music Festival. title: Mibro GS Pro2, Explorer S, GT and Fit: Which watch fits your needs? - The Gadgeteer
content:
Mibro’s GS Pro2, GS Explorer S, GT and Fit share plenty of smartwatch basics, but they make different choices about navigation, size and materials. The GS Pro2 puts dual-band GPS and running tools into an $89.99 watch. The Explorer S family brings a higher water-resistance rating and outdoor-focused construction, with titanium versions that add offline maps. GT takes the dressier round-watch route, while Fit is the lighter rectangular option. The Explorer name needs an extra look before you buy. Ceramic, Ti Standard and Ti Premium are three different configurations, and paying for titanium doesn’t make these particular watches lighter. Here’s how their published features compare, including the color and strap choices that change how much watch you’re wearing. All four families have AMOLED screens, built-in satellite positioning, Bluetooth calling, notifications and fitness tracking through the Mibro Fit app. They work with Android phones and iPhones, and Mibro lists syncing with Strava, Apple Health and Google Fit. Heart-rate, blood-oxygen, sleep and stress tracking are part of the shared package, with readings intended for general wellness information. The GS Pro2 and Explorer models also list compass, altitude and barometric tools. The useful differences are the GPS bands, navigation features, display brightness, battery ratings and what sits against your wrist. Bluetooth calling still uses a paired phone. A long daily-use battery figure also isn’t the same as continuous GPS endurance. The GS Pro2 is the straightforward choice here if you want to load a running route without spending Explorer money. Its L1+L5 dual-band GNSS supports five satellite systems, and it can keep up to 10 routes imported through the app in GPX, KML or TCX format. Forward Up and North Up views, plus vibration and screen-color deviation alerts, help you follow the route you’ve prepared. Mibro Coach adds running plans, while pace, cadence, stride length, training load and recovery-time estimates give a workout more context. The watch includes Sprint, Olympic and Free triathlon modes and a dedicated padel mode. Its 1.43-inch, 466 × 466 AMOLED display is larger in diameter than the Explorer’s screen, with a rated peak brightness of 1,200 nits. The tradeoff is fit and water-use limits. This is a 48mm watch, weighing a listed 61.6 grams with silicone or 49.6 grams with its woven strap. Mibro rates it for up to 20 days of daily use or 20 hours in GPS mode. Its 5 ATM rating comes with a specific restriction: the current product guidance limits each water exposure to 30 minutes and excludes prolonged soaking, hot showers, high heat or humidity, and steam-heavy conditions. Mibro also says to rinse it with fresh water after seawater use. Keep those limits in mind if long swims are part of your routine. Dark Gray and Light Beige have the same core specifications, and both exact Amazon variants were $89.99 when checked. Each includes silicone and woven straps. Choose the finish you prefer; this color change doesn’t buy extra navigation features. Price: $89.99 in Dark Gray or Light BeigeWhere to buy: Amazon, Dark Gray or Light Beige The ceramic Explorer S adds a nano-ceramic bezel, a reinforced-polymer body and Corning Gorilla Glass. It has a 10 ATM rating, waypoint marking and track-back navigation. The 47.8mm case is close to the GS Pro2’s diameter, but its 1.32-inch, 466 × 466 AMOLED screen is smaller. Mibro rates that display at up to 1,500 nits. Its navigation is the distinction to understand before choosing a version: the ceramic model offers waypoint guidance and track return; the titanium versions add downloaded vector maps. Ceramic still gets dual-band L1+L5 positioning, the same listed 20-day daily battery life and 25-hour GPS runtime as the titanium models, and two silicone straps. At a listed 71 grams with silicone, ceramic is also the lightest Explorer configuration here. Compared with GS Pro2, the appeal is its ceramic bezel, higher water-resistance rating, higher brightness rating despite the smaller screen, and five extra hours of claimed GPS runtime. You’re also taking on more weight. There’s a water-use conflict across the Explorer family: Mibro advertises freediving to 30 meters, while the general manual linked from these product pages warns against deep submersion, long soaking and hot water. Get Mibro’s model-specific guidance before diving. The 10 ATM rating alone isn’t permission for 100-meter dives. Price: $149.99 on Amazon; Mibro’s US store also lists $143.99Where to buy: Amazon or Mibro Ti Standard is the meaningful navigation upgrade. It adds offline vector maps that you download and transfer through Mibro Fit before heading out. Each downloaded map covers a 50 × 50-kilometer area, giving you more surrounding context than a route line alone. Route following, deviation reminders, waypoints and return navigation sit alongside that map view. The titanium construction still incorporates reinforced polymer, and this version includes gray and orange silicone straps. Its case dimensions, display, dual-band GPS, water rating and listed daily/GPS battery life match the ceramic Explorer. That makes maps the stronger reason to upgrade than a promise of better GPS accuracy or longer battery life. It also isn’t a weight-saving move: Mibro lists 76.15 grams with silicone, compared with the ceramic model’s 71 grams. If you want Explorer maps and prefer an exercise-friendly strap, Standard avoids the extra cost and weight of the bracelet version. Ti Premium, also sold as Full Ti, adds the titanium bracelet and includes a silicone alternative. It keeps the same listed display, offline-map functions, dual-band positioning, water rating and daily/GPS battery figures as Ti Standard. The higher price buys the different finish and strap configuration. The bracelet makes a noticeable difference on the specification sheet: 110 grams total, versus Standard’s 76.15 grams with silicone. For a more metal-heavy everyday look, that may be the point. For running or wearing a watch overnight, decide whether you want the bracelet enough to pay more and carry that extra weight. The name Full Ti doesn’t mean every component is titanium; Mibro still lists reinforced polymer in the construction. GT uses a 46mm round case combining 316L stainless steel and reinforced polymer, with a 1.43-inch, 466 × 466 AMOLED screen. The Silver version pairs a steel bracelet with a silicone strap; Dark Gray, listed as Black on Amazon, pairs leather with silicone. Those choices matter more than the color alone: Mibro lists 129.4 grams with the steel bracelet, 57.42 grams with leather and 63.67 grams with silicone. It has built-in five-system GPS, but the official specification explicitly says L1-only rather than the dual-band L1+L5 positioning in the GS models. Its display is rated at up to 600 nits, its water-resistance rating is 5 ATM, and the typical-use battery claim is eight days. You’re choosing the round styling and strap package over the brighter display and longer daily-use ratings in the GS range. GT and Fit also advertise AI voice or text Q&A, schedule reminders and generated watch faces. Those are extras for everyday use alongside calls, notifications and activity tracking. GT is the one to consider if you want that feature mix in a traditional round shape with a dress strap already in the box. Price: $109.99 on Amazon, with a $30 coupon shown that requires eligibility and application; Mibro’s US store lists the Silver version at $79.99Where to buy: Amazon, Silver, Amazon, Black or Mibro, Silver Fit changes the shape as well as the materials. Its aluminum-alloy and reinforced-polymer body measures 43.9 × 36.5mm, with a rectangular 1.75-inch, 390 × 450 AMOLED display. The screen’s diagonal isn’t directly comparable with the round watches’ diameters, but the narrower case is a clear alternative to their 46–48mm round bodies. Mibro’s US-store Dark Gray package includes woven and silicone straps; its Silver package includes a Milanese metal-mesh strap plus silicone. Check the included bands on your selected retailer’s listing. Mibro lists 32.79 grams with woven, 41 grams with silicone and 67.34 grams with the metal strap. On the same silicone-strap basis, Fit is substantially lighter than GT’s 63.67 grams, and its woven configuration is the lightest wearing option in this comparison. title: Are Bonds Becoming a Better Investment for Portfolios? - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. As US Treasury yields rise to the highest in decades, are bonds becoming a better investment for portfolios? “Clearly bonds look more attractive on first look,” says Christian Mueller-Glissmann, head of Asset Allocation within Goldman Sachs Research. “The challenge, of course, is it depends a lot on your investment horizon.” In the near term, longer-duration bonds may make portfolios riskier and may not provide a reliable hedge when investors shun risk. However, increasing bond allocations may make more sense for investors with longer time horizons, according to Goldman Sachs Research. Mueller-Glissmann points to four key factors to consider when allocating assets to a portfolio: the assets’ relative return, their relative risk, their correlation benefit, and their return versus cash. The relative return of bonds versus other assets is becoming more complex as there is scope for interest rates to climb higher, he says. Goldman Sachs Research’s baseline, meanwhile, is that equities’ relative return in the next few months will be boosted by earnings growth. The optimal allocation to bonds over the last five years was close to 0%, as those securities posted one of their worst five-year rolling returns in a century while equities performed strongly. “Equities can in a lot of places still cushion higher bond yields because of very strong earnings growth,” Mueller-Glissmann says. “That strong earnings growth is a bit like a buffer for higher bond yields.” Companies are reporting third-quarter earnings starting this month, and stocks have the potential to surprise to the upside. “The tech sector and artificial intelligence theme are still delivering some very strong earnings momentum, and we expect that to continue,” he says. As technology companies launch new products and services using AI, that creates potential for new revenue and monetization, Mueller-Glissmann says. At the same time, a decline in bond yields would likely be a boost to stocks as well as bond investments. “Putting it all together, the relative return to us looks better in equities,” he says. To some extent, the relative risk for bonds has improved because higher yields offer more carry, which can help cushion a portfolio against declines. But even so, the relative risk for bonds is still elevated amid Middle East tensions and uncertainty about inflation and monetary policy. Some sovereign bond issuers in Europe are also coming under pressure, as French and Italian government bond yields rise relative to those of Germany. “It's creating a more risky profile for bonds, with some of that volatility coming via the currencies,” he says. The volatility in European fixed-income securities and foreign exchange can be a “double whammy” for investors. That can also create demand for relative safe havens like US Treasuries, German bunds, and UK gilts, as those securities may benefit from rising concerns about some European government bonds. The recent correlation between bonds and stocks has not favored fixed-income assets, Mueller-Glissmann says. He notes that equity-bond correlations have been positive, with both assets in many cases rising or falling in tandem. Volatility in energy prices and hawkish central bank policy are pushing yields higher while weighing on stocks. Equity returns have been relatively flat in many markets, but Mueller-Glissmann notes that the interest-rate-sensitive parts of the stock market—such as smaller firms, and real estate and infrastructure companies—could benefit from rates relief, especially if growth concerns increase. “Over the medium term, if you have continued inflation normalization, we could see equity-bond correlations start to turn more negative,” he says. “Near-term it is more complex due to the Middle East tensions, hawkish central banks, and the AI capex boom. However, excessive tightening in financial conditions could eventually weigh on growth sentiment, potentially slowing the bond sell-off and leading to more negative equity-bond correlations.” The expected return for bonds versus cash is not necessarily attractive, according to Goldman Sachs Research. There is likely more value in shorter- to medium-term government debt because central bank policy is unlikely to drive those interest rates substantially higher, and those securities yield nearly as much as longer-term bonds, Mueller-Glissmann says. The situation could be much different over the longer term, however. “The longer your investment horizon gets, the more you need to think about a more normal allocation to bonds,” Mueller-Glissmann says. In the longer run, bonds’ relative return, relative risk, correlation benefit, and return versus cash may be substantially better than in the near term. Goldman Sachs Research uses a long-term scenario framework to predict the optimal bond allocation for the next five to 10 years based on varying macroeconomic outcomes for GDP growth, inflation, and corporate profitability. “When you look over the very long run since World War II, on average, the optimal bond allocation was actually 40%,” Mueller-Glissmann says. That aligns with a typical balanced 60/40 portfolio of 60% stocks and 40% bonds. He notes that the 10-year US Treasury yield of 5.3% is higher than the average of 4.7% over the last 250 years. “From that perspective, we are not at a bad starting point for long-run investing in bonds,” Mueller-Glissmann says. While concerns about many countries’ fiscal outlooks have risen and inflation volatility has increased, “longer-duration bond yields are reflecting that risk already a bit,” he says. Even though the outlook for the 60/40 portfolio has improved for longer-term investors, Mueller-Glissmann says he is skeptical that conditions will again be as favorable for the traditional balanced portfolio as they were before the Covid pandemic. “You need to work a bit harder within the asset classes,” he says. These portfolios may benefit from allocations to alternative assets such as real assets, hedge funds, and private equity as well as from factor investing. “Our core mantra for building a portfolio for the next decade is you need to have exposure to innovation, protection from inflation, and better risk mitigation,” Mueller-Glissmann says. Within equities, that points to favoring technology stocks and real assets, he says. In bonds, there's a stronger case for inflation-linked bonds such as Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS), with the large increase in real yields this year. Factor investing, such as low-volatility and selective high-dividend-yield stocks, can help reduce risk, because those tend to be negatively correlated with technology stocks. Commodity trading advisors (CTAs), meanwhile, have historically offered inflation protection and some protection in a crisis. This article is being provided for educational purposes only.
